vignette:
Amara was thirty-four when armed men entered the compound where she worked as a nurse in a rural clinic in South Sudan. That was eight years ago. She had been checking supplies in the back room when the shooting started-a sound she would come to know in her body before her mind could name it. The men separated the staff. What happened over the next hours existed in her memory as something both vivid and impossible, a sequence of violence and humiliation so extreme that even now, sitting in the therapist's office at forty-two, she could come to believe it had occurred to her. Sometimes she wondered if the memory belonged to someone else entirely, a story she had absorbed rather than lived. Yet her body knew. Her body remembered with perfect, treacherous clarity. The details came unbidden: the weight of hands, the smell of sweat and diesel fuel, the particular timbre of voices shouting orders in a language she understood. When she tried to sleep, these fragments would surface without warning, as real as if they were happening again in that moment.

When she finally escaped the country two years later, she carried that memory like a second skeleton. She had moved to the United States, and the work she found-assembling medical components at a factory in a sprawling industrial park outside the city-was nothing like the nursing she had trained for. The factory floor was loud and predictable in ways that felt safe at first. She could control the rhythm of it, the repetitive motions, the hiss of machinery at regular intervals. But the irony was not lost on her: she was back around medical equipment, the very instruments that had once defined her as a healer, now reduced to anonymous parts moving along a conveyor belt. It was a different form of work entirely, one that required no presence of mind, no decision-making, no responsibility for anyone's life but her own. In some ways, that was exactly what she needed. The factory work had become her refuge from the nurse she could no longer be-the steady-handed woman who had once moved through a clinic with purpose, who had had known how to calm a frightened patient, who had been trusted with lives. That woman felt impossibly distant now, as though she belonged to a different timeline altogether.

The first year in America, Amara had tried to live normally. She wore her old clothes, the bright fabrics she loved-indigo and crimson kente cloth that her mother had sent from Ghana. But in the spring, when the weather turned warm and humid, matching the season when she had been taken, her body had begun to betray her. The smell of rain on hot earth-a smell that had been present that day-would arrive on the breeze, and suddenly she could not breathe. She realized, gradually, that the bright colors themselves had become dangerous. They made her visible. Visible meant vulnerable. So she had made a deliberate choice: she packed away the kente cloth, the reds and golds and indigos that had once brought her joy, and replaced them with grays and blacks and muted neutrals. She bought clothing that was loose and shapeless, layers she could hide within. This was not merely a consequence of the weather triggers; it was an active strategy, something she did to protect herself. If she wore the bright clothes, the humid season would find her. If she wore colors that called attention, people would look at her, and looking meant seeing, and being seen meant being vulnerable to the same fate. She had stopped going outside when the weather felt similar to that season. She had stopped wearing anything that might draw a eye. Gradually, she had narrowed the world. At home, she listened. Always listening. For footsteps on the stairs, for the sound of a key in the lock, for voices that might indicate someone was coming. Her apartment was on the second floor, and she had memorized every creak of the building, every sound that meant safety and every sound that meant danger. When her ex-husband had tried to visit last year-a man named Kofi-she had felt her entire body tense, flooded with a fear that made no logical sense. He was not one of them. But her body did not distinguish. Her body reacted to danger before her mind could catch up, before she could remind herself that she was safe, that this was America, that it was only a familiar name.

At the factory, her supervisor had begun to notice the changes. The woman who had arrived two years ago in bright fabrics had transformed into someone gray and unremarkable, someone who seemed to be trying to disappear into the machinery itself. When he asked if she was all right, she had said yes. She had not mentioned that she flinched at every unexpected sound, that her coworkers had begun to notice how she startled at the normal noises of the production line-the pneumatic hiss of machinery, the clang of metal on metal. She had not mentioned that she had stopped attending the evening shifts because darkness made the listening worse, and she had been quietly demoted to day work, a consequence no one discussed but everyone understood. The demotion meant less pay, fewer hours, less stability. It meant she had to rely more heavily on her sister for help with rent. It meant she was no longer the independent woman she had been. The factory floor, which had once felt like a place of refuge, had become another site of failure-another reminder that she could not function normally, could not hold her ground, could not be trusted to show up as her whole self.

What frightened Amara most was that her body no longer felt like her own. She could not trust it to react appropriately, to distinguish between real danger and the ghosts of danger. She was no longer capable of the things that had once defined her-the steadiness, the presence of mind, the ability to help others without falling apart. The world had shown itself to be a place where men could take what they wanted, and no amount of vigilance could prevent that. She had come to believe that she would spend the rest of her life listening for footsteps, jumping at sounds, trying to disappear into neutral colors and careful silence. Last month, her sister had finally convinced her to call someone. She had made the appointment. She was here. And what she was most afraid of, more than anything, was that this was simply who she was now-that the nurse she had been, the woman who had once run toward people in crisis, was gone forever, replaced by someone smaller, someone afraid, someone who could no longer be trusted with the work that had once given her life meaning.

# Amara

Amara was thirty-four when armed men entered the compound where she worked as a nurse in a rural clinic in South Sudan. That was eight years ago. She had been checking supplies in the back room when the shooting started—a sound she would come to know in her body before her mind could name it. The men separated the staff. What happened over the next hours existed in her memory as something both vivid and impossible, a sequence of violence and humiliation so extreme that even now, sitting in the therapist's office, she could not quite believe it had occurred to her. Sometimes she wondered if the memory belonged to someone else entirely, a story she had absorbed rather than lived. Yet her body knew. Her body remembered with perfect, treacherous clarity.

When she finally escaped the country two years later, she carried that memory like a second skeleton. She had moved to the United States, found work at a factory assembling medical components—ironic, she thought sometimes, that she was back around medical equipment but in a different form of captivity. The factory floor was loud and predictable. She could control it. What she could not control was the world outside.

The first year in America, Amara had tried to live normally. She wore her old clothes, the bright fabrics she loved. But in the spring, when the weather turned warm and humid, matching the season when she had been taken, her body had begun to betray her. The smell of rain on hot earth—a smell that had been present that day—would arrive on the breeze, and suddenly she could not breathe. She had stopped wearing the clothes associated with that time. She had stopped going outside when the weather felt similar. Gradually, she had narrowed the world.

At home, she listened. Always listening. For footsteps on the stairs, for the sound of a key in the lock, for voices that might indicate someone was coming. Her apartment was on the second floor, and she had memorized every creak of the building, every sound that meant safety and every sound that meant danger. When her ex-husband had tried to visit last year—a man named Kofi, a name that appeared sometimes in conversation—she had felt her entire body tense, flooded with a fear that made no logical sense. He was not one of them. But her body did not distinguish. Her body reacted to danger before her mind could catch up, before she could remind herself that she was safe, that this was America, that it was only a name.

She had taken to wearing heavy makeup, layers of it, as though she could paint over what had happened to her skin, make herself unrecognizable even to herself. At the factory, her supervisor had asked if she was all right. She had said yes. She had not mentioned that she flinched at every unexpected sound, that her coworkers had begun to notice how she startled at the normal noises of the production line—the pneumatic hiss of machinery, the clang of metal on metal. She had not mentioned that she had stopped attending the evening shifts because darkness made the listening worse, and she had been quietly demoted to day work, a consequence no one discussed but everyone understood.

What frightened Amara most was that her body no longer felt like her own. She could not trust it to react appropriately, to distinguish between real danger and the ghosts of danger. She was no longer capable of the things that had once defined her—the steadiness, the presence of mind, the ability to help others without falling apart. The world had shown itself to be a place where men could take what they wanted, and no amount of vigilance could prevent that. She was forty-two now, and she had come to believe that she would spend the rest of her life listening for footsteps, jumping at sounds, trying to paint over the past with makeup and mental distraction. Last month, her sister had finally convinced her to call someone. She had made the appointment. She was here. And what she was most afraid of, more than anything, was that this was simply who she was now.
